raw_graphql_pull_request.body:
## Motivation

`jit-kernel-unit-test-amd` has been red on `main` since #40785 merged. Every run that has executed the job since has failed identically — #40785's own run, two on #34537, and one on an unrelated branch, all reporting `30732 / 65536` mismatched elements at the same index. The job only runs when a PR touches `python/sglang/kernels/`, so most PRs skip it and it went unnoticed.

Full evidence in #42981.

## Modifications

torch's `float8_e4m3fn` cast saturates to its max finite value. `float8_e4m3fnuz` has no infinity, so `fp8e4m3fnuz_from_fp32_value` returns NaN (`0x80`) for every magnitude at or above 256.0. Triton's cast saturates on both types, so the fused commit kernel from #40785 matches eager on CUDA and diverges on gfx94x.

This is not only a test problem. `set_kv_buffer_prefix_valid` has a fused path and an eager fallback, and on ROCm they now write different bytes for the same input — the fallback writes NaN into a committed KV slot, which poisons attention for that slot on every later read.

Rather than have the test chase whichever cast runs, this makes saturation the defined contract and clamps before the FP8 cast in all three places:

- `cache_move.py` — the kernel clamps, with the limit passed as a `tl.constexpr`; NaN falls through both `tl.where` arms. Two vector ops added to a memory-bound kernel.
- `memory_pool.py` — the eager fallback clamps identically, so the two production paths agree.
- `test/kernels/prefix_valid.py` — the shared oracle clamps identically.

The limit is `torch.finfo(fp8).max`, not the conservative `fp8_max` constant (224.0 on fnuz): clamping at 224.0 would pull values that eager rounds to 240.0 down a step.

All three are no-ops on CUDA, where the eager cast already saturates to 448.

## Test plan

`jit-kernel-unit-test-amd` on MI300 / ROCm 10: **42/42 files passed** ([job](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/37648241557/job/113082433719)), including `test_prefix_valid_fp8.py` and `test_prefix_valid_fp8_pool.py`. For reference, the same job on current `main` fails at 6/42 with 30732/65536 mismatched elements.

An earlier revision of this branch clamped in FP32, which turned the `bf16/fp16 -> fp8` cast into `fp32 -> fp8`; those lower to different conversions and left 2/65536 elements off by one FP8 subnormal step at fp16 with a host scalar scale. Clamping in the source dtype restores the original lowering, and that is the version here.

Still red on this PR, all reproducing on #40785 or unrelated to this path:

- `stage-b-test-1-gpu-small-amd (7)` — MiniMax sparse decode kernel requests 128 KiB LDS against a 64 KiB limit (`OutOfResources`), same partition red on #40785.
- `stage-b-test-1-gpu-small-amd-mi35x (1)` — red on #40785.
- `extra-a-test-1-gpu-small-amd` — `test_e2e_spec_eagle.py`; the server stops responding mid-stream (`RemoteDisconnected`), with no CUDA/HIP fault, scheduler exception or OOM in the log. That test runs `kv_cache_dtype=auto`, so `self.dtype` is not FP8 and neither the fused branch nor the eager clamp in this PR is reached — the non-FP8 commit path goes through `set_kv_buffer_prefix_valid_tiled`, which is untouched here. The same job is also red on #40785, on a different test.
- NPU jobs — `set_kv_buffer_prefix_valid` returns early for non-CUDA/non-HIP before reaching any line this PR touches.

If you would rather the kernel reproduce eager's `e4m3fnuz` NaN-on-overflow instead of saturating, I can invert the patch — but that writes NaN into the KV cache on AMD and diverges from the CUDA path, so saturation looks like the better contract.

## Checklist

- [x] Format your code according to the [Format code with pre-commit](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#format-code-with-pre-commit).
- [x] Follow the SGLang code style [guidance](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#code-style-guidance).

nodes.body: @JiaFengYu please help review fix introduced by your pr https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/40785 cc: @BBuf

Thanks — both applied in `21ae7868`.

**Clamp simplification.** Confirmed before changing it: `launch_clamp_scalar` in `aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/TensorCompare.cu` returns the input early for NaN, and the comment there is explicit that this is deliberate — *"Propagate nan, which doesn't propagate automatically for ROCm"*. The CPU kernel leaves it to `std::min`/`std::max`, which return the NaN operand. So the `isnan`/`where` pair was redundant on both backends; it is now just `value.clamp(-limit, limit)`.

**Pool test.** Added `test_eager_fallback_saturates_overflow`, no new file. It leaves `k_scale_float` unresolved so `_resolve_fused_scale` returns `None` and the commit takes the eager writer, then asserts against literals rather than the helper: overflow lands on `±torch.finfo(fp8_dtype).max`, an input NaN stays NaN, an in-range value stays exact, and the uncommitted slots keep their original bytes. Since the expected values do not come from `saturate_to_fp8_range`, a regression in the helper cannot move the assertion with it — which was your point.

Both changes need a CI pass to confirm; I will follow up if the MI300 job disagrees.

The saturation contract makes sense here: finite overflow should not introduce NaNs into committed KV slots, and the fused writer and eager fallback should agree. Using the representable FP8 limit and preserving the source dtype before the final cast both look right.

I checked the CI for `eaebedfc`: the MI300 JIT job passed all 42 test files, including both prefix-valid FP8 test files, and the CUDA kernel jobs passed too.

Two non-blocking suggestions:

- In `saturate_to_fp8_range`, could we simplify this to `value.clamp(-limit, limit)`? PyTorch's CUDA/ROCm scalar clamp implementation already preserves input NaNs. If that also holds for the supported PyTorch versions, the explicit `isnan` and `where` add unnecessary eager operations and intermediate tensors.
- Could we add explicit overflow assertions in the existing pool test, forcing the eager fallback? The oracle now uses the same saturation helper as production, while the current fallback cases use small random inputs. Checking that overflow produces `+/-torch.finfo(fp8_dtype).max`, input NaNs remain NaN, and uncommitted slots stay unchanged, without using the helper to construct the expected values, would independently pin down the new contract. No new test file is needed.

+@triton.jit
+def _saturate_to_fp8_range(val, FP8_MAX: tl.constexpr, DTYPE: tl.constexpr):
+    """Clamp into the FP8 range, leaving NaN untouched.
+
+    Mirrors ``saturate_to_fp8_range`` on the eager side. Comparisons against
+    NaN are false, so a NaN input falls through both ``tl.where`` arms and
+    still converts to the FP8 NaN encoding.
+
+    Each arm casts back to ``DTYPE`` because the FP8_MAX literal is FP32 and
+    would otherwise widen the result. Keeping the value in the source dtype
+    matters: the final cast to FP8 must start from the same type it did before
+    this clamp existed, or it can lower to a different conversion with its own
+    tie-breaking in the FP8 subnormal range. The limit itself is exact in
+    BF16/FP16/FP32, so the round trip loses nothing.
+    """
+    val = tl.where(val > FP8_MAX, FP8_MAX, val).to(DTYPE)
+    return tl.where(val < -FP8_MAX, -FP8_MAX, val).to(DTYPE)
+
+

+def saturate_to_fp8_range(value: torch.Tensor, dtype: torch.dtype) -> torch.Tensor:
+    """Clamp to the representable range of ``dtype``, leaving NaN untouched.
+
+    The two FP8 types disagree on overflow. ``float8_e4m3fn`` saturates to its
+    max finite value, but ``float8_e4m3fnuz`` has no infinity, so its eager cast

+    gives both types the saturating behaviour, which keeps the fused Triton
+    commit kernel and the eager fallback byte-identical on ROCm and avoids
+    writing NaN into a committed KV slot.

+    conservative ``fp8_max`` above: clamping at 224.0 would pull values that
+    eager rounds to 240.0 down a step and lose precision.
+    """
+    limit = torch.finfo(dtype).max
+    # clamp propagates NaN rather than folding it onto a bound: the CUDA/ROCm
+    # kernel returns the input early for NaN, and the CPU one leaves it to
+    # std::min/std::max, which return the NaN operand.
+    return value.clamp(-limit, limit)
+
